newsitem.title: ITALY: Deforestation slows, but not out of woods yet - FAO.
newsitem.headline: Deforestation slows, but not out of woods yet - FAO.

text.p: The U.N.'s Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) said on Friday that the pace of global deforestation was slowing but increasing population pressures meant forests would continue to shrink for the next decade.

David Harcharik, head of FAO's forestry department, told a news conference ahead of a four-day meeting of experts to assess sustainable development that natural forests in developing countries decreased by 13.7 million hectares (33.85 million acres) a year in 1990-95.
That compared with an annual fall of 15.5 million hectares (38.3 million acres) between 1980 and 1990 -- an improvement of some 12 percent.

But Harcharik, who is also assistant director-general of the Rome-based agency, said it would be foolish to think the problem was over, adding sophisticated statistical procedures being developed would provide a clearer picture of the trend.
He stressed that, globally, natural forests and plantations were still shrinking by some 11.3 million hectares (27.9 million acres) a year.
"We would like to say we should be hopeful, but the area we are talking about is twice the size of Italy which has been lost in 1990-95. It's still a very high rate," Harcharik said.
"We are optimistic we are going in the right direction but there is still a long, long way to go."

Senior forestry officials from around the world will meet at FAO's headquarters from Monday to review progress on sustainable forestry and assess the impact of a food security plan of action concluded at FAO's World Food Summit last November.

FAO monitors the global situation and implements some special forestry programmes but is not responsible for forestry management in individual countries. It will release its second major bi-annual study on the state of the world's forests.

Harcharik said that, in the developed world, lower population growth and higher agricultural development meant pressures on forest land to be converted for other uses had eased. Total forests grew by some 1.8 million hectares (4.5 million acres) a year in 1990-95.

"Therefore...there is going to have to be a decline in the population rate and an increase in economic development including agricultural productivity (in the developing world) as has taken place in the north," he said.

FAO reckons world food production will increase by an annual 1.8 percent until the year 2010, needing 90 million hectares (222 million acres) of extra agricultural land -- half of that coming from forests.
"So the trend for the next decade or so will continue to show a decrease in forests," said Marc Rene de Montalembert, director of FAO's forestry policy and planning division.
Despite the acute problem of tropical deforestation, Harcharik said the solution did not lie with developed world consumers avoiding anything made with tropical wood.

"We should try to help countries better manage their forests," he said. "If we put in place barriers to trade and disincentives to sales of some products it creates an incentive to convert these forests to other more productive uses."
